title: dutch power moratoriums highlight challenge facing grid operators  reeii 2026 06 16
text:
June 16 - As AI demand surges, moratoriums on new grid connections in the Netherlands underline the urgent need for grid expansions and enhancements across Europe and the United States.
The Netherlands has imposed localised bans on new connection of power generation and non-residential loads since 2022. Next month, this ban will be extended to new residential connections in the city of Utrecht.
The moratoriums are holding back the energy transition as well as wider economic growth offered by new data centers and other large loads.
Grid operators in the Netherlands have been unable to keep up with a surge in renewable energy projects, partly fuelled by Europe's ban on Russian gas imports following its invasion of Ukraine, and the more recent surge in data centre demand.
Dutch renewable energy capacity doubled between 2019 and 2023 to 36 GW, representing 41% of total power generation.
There was 630 MW of data centre capacity under construction this month, 2.4 GW under development and 7.9 GW of new applications, according to national grid operator TenneT. By 2030, data centres will consume 15% of national power generation, compared with 5% currently, the grid operator said.
Growing renewable energy capacity and electrification of energy demand has increased power market volatility and the roll-out of flexibility tools like energy storage has not kept up with rising demand, Ivo van Dam, Chief Operating Officer at BayWa r.e. subsidiary GroenLeven, told Reuters Events.
This is “the underlying reason the situation feels so acute in the Netherlands today,” van Dam said.
CHART: Netherlands power generation by source
Grid expansion projects can take many years, due to long and complex permitting procedures, a lack of available land and long component lead times.
According to TenneT, transmission projects can take up to 12 years to be completed and over 50% of transmission projects needed by 2030 still await permits.
The Netherlands is densely populated and many grid expansion projects have also been unable to secure construction permits as nitrogen oxide emissions (NOx) hit regulatory limits on the back of high agriculture sector emissions.
TenneT is rolling out a range of measures to fast-track priority grid projects and optimise existing grid infrastructure but the use of moratoriums show how more proactive investments are crucial.
In 2025, TenneT invested 14.8 billion euros ($17.2 billion) in grid improvements but estimates 1.2 trillion euros is needed by 2040.
“Without timely grid expansion, connection delays and congestion costs will increase," TenneT European Political Affairs Specialist Mark van der Boor told Reuters Events.
Grids under pressure
Dutch authorities are streamlining critical grid projects to bring more capacity online.
TenneT and the Dutch government have listed 105 critical grid projects for joint public-private investments that tackle key obstacles in a bid to reduce lead times by 40% to 50%.
The EU’s Permitting Directive implemented in December 2025 includes measures to exempt grid projects from environmental procedures but it could take time to impact project timelines.
European grid operators must focus on “forward-looking frameworks that prioritise mature and system-relevant projects” rather than a ‘first come, first served’ approach, a spokesperson for Elia Group, a transmission group operating in Belgium and Germany, told Reuters Events.

In another measure, TenneT identified 9.1 GW of existing Dutch grid capacity that can be used during off-peak hours with Time-Dependent Transmission Right contracts.
TenneT has also introduced use-it-or-lose-it grid capacity principles and connection processes with shorter signing windows and front-loaded payments, van Dam noted.
These “create more discipline and unlock additional capacity from existing infrastructure” but the Dutch system still needs to be adapted for less predictable generation and demand, he said.
Battery storage can support system stability by providing balancing, voltage support and inertia services, the Elia Group spokesperson said.
Grid operators are now focusing on "optimising how and where these assets operate,” the spokesperson said.
TenneT has also implemented a number of grid enhancing technologies such as dynamic line rating, which it says unlocks up to 30% more capacity.
The grid operator is also improving congestion management and introducing demand flexibility initiatives that allow users to switch consumption.
Offshore connections
North Sea offshore wind expansions and international interconnectors will help Netherlands and other Western European countries manage grid congestion going forward.
According to TenneT, North Sea offshore wind capacity could reach 300 GW by 2050, providing 40% of Europe’s electricity.
Coastal countries are developing hybrid interconnectors that connect offshore wind projects to multiple countries and enable cross-border electricity trade.
For instance, TenneT and National Grid Ventures are planning to install a new LionLink interconnector that would connect a new 2 GW Dutch offshore wind farm to the Netherlands and the UK by the early 2030s.
Mechanisms are needed that share the costs of these new lines between the countries that develop them or benefit from them, van der Boor said.

Another option for the Netherlands is to introduce a Capacity Remuneration Mechanism (CRM) that pays generators, energy storage and demand-response assets to guarantee grid availability during peak demand periods.
Belgium has introduced a CRM but Netherlands has refrained in order to avoid subsidising fossil fuel plants.
The challenges in the Netherlands show that grid operators must treat flexibility as a structural component of the system from the outset, build localised congestion instruments, and align the pace of market redesign with the physical deployment of assets, van Dam said.
The main lesson is that “Europe should not wait until congestion becomes critical and should proactively invest in grid expansion,” Robert Ranke, Senior Advisor Public & Regulatory Affairs at energy utility Vattenfall Netherlands, told Reuters Events.
